c9:p31:
# Context

After Mr. and Mrs. Boffin decide to adopt an orphan child in memory of young John Harmon, they discuss practical methods for finding a suitable candidate. This passage shows their deliberation process as they reject advertising in newspapers due to concerns about attracting too many applicants, then settle on consulting their clergyman for a recommendation. The passage concludes with their decision to make formal visits of state to both the clergyman and Miss Bella Wilfer, for which Mrs. Boffin's carriage is prepared.
c10:p0: This passage opens the chapter describing the wedding preparations at the Veneering household. It introduces the main event—the marriage of Sophronia Akershem and Alfred Lammle—and establishes the Veneerings' role as hosts. The Analytical (the butler) is characterized as perpetually objecting to household matters, while flowers are being delivered for tomorrow's wedding breakfast, setting the scene for the elaborate social occasion that follows.
c10:p1: This passage appears early in the chapter and introduces Alfred Lammle, the "mature young gentleman" who is marrying Sophronia Akershem. It serves as a satirical critique of Lammle's character and the Victorian obsession with wealth derived from stock market speculation (Shares), establishing him as a superficial fortune-hunter defined entirely by his involvement in financial trafficking rather than by any genuine accomplishment, character, or principles. The passage foreshadows the revelation later in the chapter that both bride and groom have married under false pretenses regarding their actual fortunes.
c10:p2: This passage occurs as Twemlow puzzles over the Veneerings' claims of long-standing friendship with the bride and groom, Sophronia Akershem and Alfred Lammle, before their wedding breakfast. # Context for Chunk

This is a poem excerpt that Mr. Wegg recites to Mr. Boffin when declining what he initially misinterprets as an offer to be pensioned off. Wegg uses the verse about "little Edmund the poor Peasant boy" as a theatrical response expressing his reluctance to accept charity, claiming he would prefer to wander into the world rather than be dependent on Mr. Boffin's money. The poem serves as part of Wegg's manipulative and self-pitying performance during negotiations over his new employment arrangement as keeper of the Bower.
c15:p99: Mr. Boffin offers Wegg money to give up his street stall, but Wegg misinterprets this as being pensioned off. c16:p0: This chunk introduces the Secretary (John Rokesmith) and his exemplary work ethic upon being employed by Mr. Boffin, the Golden Dustman. It establishes his diligence, thoroughness, and commitment to mastering all aspects of his employer's business affairs from the outset of his engagement.

c35:p0: This is the opening passage of a scene where Riah, a Jewish moneylender, visits Miss Jenny Wren, the dolls' dressmaker, on a foggy evening. c35:p1: Riah the Jew visits Miss Jenny Wren, the dolls' dressmaker, at her home on a foggy evening. He arrives at her doorstep and she greets him, having been waiting for him by her fire.

c35:p7: Riah visits Miss Jenny Wren at her home. As they prepare to leave together, Riah offers to carry a large key for her, but Jenny refuses, explaining that she intentionally wears her pocket on her higher side to balance her lopsided body.
c35:p8: Riah the Jew and Miss Jenny Wren, the dolls' dressmaker, depart from her home after she locks the door. c35:p9: Miss Wren and Riah the Jew are walking through the fog together, with Miss Wren playfully addressing Riah as her "fairy godmother." c35:p10: Riah and Miss Jenny Wren are walking through the fog together. Jenny has just compared Riah to a fairy godmother from storybooks. Riah now playfully asks whether Jenny imagines he could change other things besides people, continuing their imaginative, whimsical conversation.

c35:p12: Miss Jenny Wren imaginatively asks Riah (her "godmother") to use his magical powers to transform a dirty stone into a coach and six. Riah readily agrees to this whimsical fantasy.
c35:p13: Miss Jenny Wren asks Riah, whom she playfully calls her "godmother" (like a fairy godmother), to magically transform her child, who has been behaving badly, refusing to work for ten days, and suffering from disturbing hallucinations about being thrown into a furnace.
c35:p14: Riah expresses concern when Miss Jenny Wren asks him, in her playful fairy godmother fantasy, to magically transform her troublesome child who has been idle and experiencing psychological distress for ten days.
c35:p15: Miss Jenny Wren walks through the fog with Riah, an elderly Jewish man she calls her "godmother." She playfully asks him to use his magical powers to change her troublesome child, describing his recent dangerous behavior and refusal to obey her commands.
c35:p16: Riah and Miss Jenny Wren are walking through the fog together. c35:p17: Miss Jenny Wren, a disabled doll's dressmaker, is walking through the fog with Riah, an elderly Jewish man. c35:p18: Miss Jenny Wren asks Riah, her "godmother," to magically fix her crippled back and legs, speaking without complaint despite her physical suffering.

c35:p22: Miss Jenny Wren is walking through the fog with Riah, an elderly Jewish man she calls her "godmother." c36:p0: Riderhood, a disreputable river character, has been pulled from the water after being struck by a steamer. His seemingly lifeless body is being brought into Miss Abbey Potterson's inn to be revived. This opening describes the physical difficulty of carrying his rigid corpse up the stairs to her bedroom.
c36:p1: Riderhood has been pulled from the river after being struck by a steamer. Miss Abbey brings his unconscious, dripping body to her first-floor bedroom, then immediately orders messengers to fetch a doctor and his daughter Pleasant.
c36:p2: Riderhood, a disreputable river worker, has been pulled from the water after being struck by a steamer. He is brought to Miss Abbey Potterson's inn, where a doctor arrives to examine him. Though no one respects Riderhood himself, the assembled crowd becomes deeply invested in attempting to revive him, driven by a profound human interest in preserving life itself rather than any regard for the man personally.
c36:p3: Riderhood has been pulled from the river after being struck by a steamer. As doctors and onlookers work to revive him, Tom Tootle provides his eyewitness account of the accident, explaining that Riderhood was carelessly maneuvering his boat when the steamer struck and destroyed the vessel, though Riderhood himself remains intact.
c36:p4: Riderhood, a disliked riverman, has been pulled from the river after being struck by a steamer. He is brought to Miss Abbey Potterson's inn, where a doctor and several regular customers attempt to revive him through artificial respiration. Captain Joey, an old-fashioned customer, offers absurd medical advice suggesting the body be hung upside down like butcher's meat and rolled on casks. Miss Abbey angrily ejects him from the room for his ridiculous suggestions.
c36:p5: A drowned man (Riderhood) has been brought to Miss Abbey's inn and resuscitation efforts are underway. After Captain Joey is ejected for his unhelpful suggestions, the doctor continues working with the remaining three regular customers—Bob Glamour, William Williams, and Jonathan—while Miss Abbey leaves the room to wait downstairs with the Jew and Miss Jenny Wren for news of whether Riderhood will survive.
c36:p6: This passage reflects the narrator's meditation on Riderhood's uncertain state between life and death during the resuscitation efforts. It captures the moment of profound suspense as the doctor and attendants work to revive him, emphasizing the solemnity and mystery surrounding whether Riderhood will survive or perish, and the emotional weight this uncertainty places on those present.
c36:p7: The doctor is carefully monitoring the nearly-drowned Riderhood's body during artificial resuscitation efforts at Miss Abbey Potterson's inn, watching intently for any sign of life returning to the unconscious man.
c36:p8: This single word "No." is part of a series of repeated negations where the doctor, during his examination of the drowned man Riderhood, checks for signs of life. The doctor asks himself a series of questions—"Did that eyelid tremble?" "Did that nostril twitch?" c36:p9: The doctor performs a series of careful examinations to detect signs of life in the drowned man Riderhood, asking himself a series of questions—"Did that eyelid tremble?" "Did that nostril twitch?"—as he attempts to revive him through artificial respiration.
c36:p10: The doctor repeatedly checks for signs of life in the drowning victim Riderhood—asking silently if his eyelid trembles, if his nostril twitches, if there is any flutter under his hand on the chest—receiving "No" as the answer each time before finally detecting a token of life.
c36:p11: A doctor attempts to revive the drowned body of Rogue Riderhood through artificial respiration, repeatedly checking for signs of life by examining his breathing, pulse, and chest movement.
c36:p12: The doctor repeatedly checks for signs of life in the drowned man Riderhood—asking whether his eyelid trembled, his nostril twitched, or his heart flutters—receiving "No" as the answer each time before finally detecting a token of life.
c36:p13: The doctor attempts to revive the drowned man Riderhood through artificial respiration, repeatedly checking for signs of life—watching for eye tremors, nostril twitches, and chest flutter—before finally detecting a token of life that inspires the assembled men to tears.
c36:p14: A drowned man, Riderhood, is being revived at Miss Abbey's inn. c36:p15: This passage describes Riderhood's struggle to regain consciousness after being pulled from the river. c36:p16: Riderhood, a disreputable riverfront character, has been pulled from the water after being struck by a steamer. c36:p18: Miss Abbey's reassuring remark to Pleasant Riderhood after the drowned man (Riderhood, Pleasant's father) is brought to her inn. She is explaining that she helped revive him without knowing his identity, and would have done the same regardless of who he was.
c36:p19: Pleasant Riderhood, the daughter of the drowned man Riderhood, arrives at Miss Abbey Potterson's inn after being summoned. c36:p21: Pleasant Riderhood, the daughter of the drowned man being revived by the doctor, gains composure and begins assisting in her father's resuscitation efforts, transitioning from emotional distress to practical helpfulness by anticipating the doctor's needs and eventually supporting his head during the revival attempt.
c36:p22: Riderhood has been pulled from the river, apparently drowned. After intensive resuscitation efforts by the doctor and patrons of Miss Abbey's establishment, he shows signs of life. c36:p23: Riderhood, a disreputable man, has been pulled from the river after being struck by a steamer. Miss Abbey brings him to her bedroom where the doctor and several men work to resuscitate him. c36:p24: Riderhood has been rescued after being struck by a steamer and nearly drowned. After intense efforts at resuscitation, he begins to show signs of life. The doctor declares him recovered, prompting emotional reactions from the bystanders who had been moved by the struggle to save him, even though they normally despise Riderhood. This moment represents the peak of their compassion before their feelings harden again as Riderhood regains consciousness.
c36:p25: Riderhood has been successfully resuscitated after nearly drowning in the river. As he regains consciousness, he begins to show signs of awareness and awareness of his surroundings.
c36:p26: Pleasant Riderhood informs her father Rogue Riderhood, who has been pulled from the river after being struck by a steamer, of his location as he regains consciousness following revival efforts by Miss Abbey Potterson and others at her establishment.
c36:p27: Riderhood regains consciousness after nearly drowning and being revived through the doctor's efforts. c36:p28: After Riderhood is resuscitated and shows signs of life, the people who worked to save him—moved by the spark of human consciousness itself—experience a profound shift in sentiment. The chapter illustrates how their initial sympathy was conditional upon his unconsciousness and helplessness.
c36:p29: Riderhood has been revived after nearly drowning. c36:p30: Riderhood has been rescued from drowning and revived through the efforts of the doctor and several men at Miss Abbey's establishment. c36:p31: A group of men who have worked to revive the drowning victim Riderhood express their disappointment as he regains consciousness, with Bob Glamour voicing pessimism about whether Riderhood will reform or improve his character following his near-death experience.
c36:p32: After Riderhood is revived from near-drowning, the men who helped save him express disappointment that he survived, suggesting he'll waste his second chance at life just as he wasted his first.
c36:p33: After Riderhood is revived from near-drowning, the men who assisted in his resuscitation express their disappointment that he has survived. Jonathan's remark cynically dismisses any hope that the ordeal will improve Riderhood's character or behavior.
c36:p34: Riderhood has been successfully revived from drowning, but as he regains consciousness and his true nature reasserts itself, the men who worked so hard to save him grow cold and distant. c36:p35: After Riderhood is revived from near-death by drowning, the men who worked to save him gradually lose interest and withdraw their sympathy. Miss Abbey attempts to restore morale by praising their efforts and offering them refreshment at her expense.
c36:p36: After successfully reviving the drowned man Riderhood, the gathered men and Miss Abbey leave to have refreshments at her expense, leaving his daughter Pleasant alone to watch over him as he recovers.
c36:p37: Riderhood has been revived after nearly drowning, and the initial sympathy for him quickly fades as he regains consciousness and displays his characteristic gruff, sullen nature. Bob Gliddery comments on Riderhood's pale, sickly appearance while the revived man remains unconscious.
c36:p38: Pleasant Riderhood watches her father recover from drowning at Miss Abbey Potterson's inn. Bob Gliddery comments that her father's appearance looks odd, and Pleasant faintly nods in response to his observation.
c36:p39: Pleasant's father, Riderhood, has been pulled from the river after an accident with a steamer and is being revived at Miss Abbey Potterson's house. c36:p40: Riderhood has been revived after nearly drowning, and the men who helped save him are now disappointed by his survival and cold toward him. c36:p41: Riderhood has been revived after nearly drowning. Bob Gliddery comments to Pleasant Riderhood about the irony that her father, who was previously banned from Miss Abbey's establishment, has now been brought back there unconscious and is being cared for by the very people who dislike him.
c36:p42: Riderhood, a disreputable man, has been pulled from the river and revived at Miss Abbey Potterson's establishment. c36:p43: Pleasant Riderhood, the daughter of the revived drowning victim Riderhood, maintains a small measure of pride about her father's presence at Miss Abbey's establishment, but Bob Gliddery cynically reminds her that Riderhood was only admitted because he arrived unconscious and dying—Miss Abbey had previously banned him from the house entirely.
c36:p44: Pleasant Riderhood watches her father Riderhood recover from drowning at Miss Abbey's inn. c36:p45: Riderhood has been revived from near-death by drowning, and the initial sympathy and effort to save him quickly evaporates once he regains consciousness. c36:p46: Riderhood, after being pulled from the river and revived through the efforts of Miss Abbey's customers and the doctor, begins to regain consciousness. Though the onlookers had wept at the spark of life returning to him, their sympathy evaporates as he recovers, and they withdraw their care. c36:p47: Riderhood has just been pulled from the river after being struck by a steamer. The doctor and others have worked to revive him, and he has regained consciousness. The doctor now asks this opening question as Riderhood sits up in bed, beginning to recover.
c36:p48: Riderhood, who has been revived after nearly drowning in the river, regains consciousness and responds irritably to the doctor's inquiry about his condition, showing no gratitude for being saved and returning to his characteristically unpleasant disposition.
c36:p49: Riderhood, a disreputable man, has been pulled from the river after being struck by a steamer. Miss Abbey's staff and regular customers work to revive him. c36:p50: Riderhood has been revived after nearly drowning in the river. The doctor expresses hope that this escape will have a good moral effect on him, but Riderhood responds with a gruff, unintelligible growl, rejecting what his daughter understands as unwanted moralizing or "Poll-Parroting."
c36:p51: Riderhood has been revived after nearly drowning and is regaining consciousness. As he recovers, his ungrateful and surly nature returns, disappointing those who had worked to save him. c36:p52: Riderhood, having recovered consciousness after nearly drowning, questions his daughter Pleasant about the vessel that struck him down, asking if it was a steamer before demanding legal compensation.
c36:p53: Pleasant Riderhood responds affirmatively to her father Riderhood when he asks if it was a steamer that struck him down in the river, moments after he regains consciousness at Miss Abbey Potterson's inn.

Wegg is attempting to extract information from Venus about his romantic troubles with Pleasant Riderhood. After Venus has reluctantly revealed her name and mentioned acquiring a parrot from her, Wegg reminds Venus of a cryptic remark he made during their earlier conversation—that Venus had "got up there" but then said "Never mind"—referring to the shelf where Venus keeps the parrot, which he has never prepared and remains dried and unused.
c40:p94: Venus laments the parrot he purchased from Pleasant Riderhood, which remains unprepared in his shop. This reveals his emotional state following his rejection by her and his inability to move forward with his life or work.
c40:p95: Wegg prepares to leave Venus's taxidermy shop after Venus has revealed his lovesick despair over Pleasant Riderhood. Wegg, having lost interest in Venus's emotional troubles and now focused on his secret scheme with the will they've discovered, adjusts his wooden leg in preparation for departure.
c40:p96: Wegg leaves Venus's shop with the will he discovered, reflecting on his regret at bringing Venus into their scheme. He second-guesses the partnership, worries about dissolving it without financial loss, and congratulates himself on his luck while traveling to Boffin's house.
c40:p97: After Wegg and Venus reach an agreement to blackmail Mr. Boffin using the newly discovered will, Wegg leaves Venus's shop with the hat-box. He reflects on his partnership with Venus, reconsidering whether involving him was worthwhile. Despite his doubts about the partnership, Wegg is drawn to Mr. Boffin's house to revel in his newfound power over the wealthy man and his family, feeling a malevolent satisfaction in possessing knowledge that could destroy their fortune.
c40:p98: Silas Wegg, after leaving Venus's shop with a will he discovered that could challenge Mr. Boffin's inheritance, positions himself outside Boffin's house to savor his newfound power over the wealthy man, exulting in his ability to blackmail him.
c41:p0: This passage opens the chapter with a satirical address to government officials and charitable boards, using the metaphor of a heap of ashes to criticize the slow and inadequate removal of social failures and poor relief measures. It serves as the thematic prelude to the subsequent narrative about Old Betty Higden's desperate flight from parish authority and the cruelty of the workhouse system.
c41:p1: This passage is Dickens's scathing authorial commentary on the poor laws and charitable institutions. It directly follows the opening description of removing a heap of ashes and serves as a moral indictment of how the established systems for relieving poverty actually harm the deserving poor while failing to deter professional paupers. The passage criticizes the hypocrisy of having wealth available for relief yet driving the genuinely needy to despair and death. It sets the ideological context for the subsequent narrative of Old Betty Higden, whose fear of the workhouse and parish system will drive much of the chapter's action.
c41:p2: This passage introduces Old Betty Higden's character and her fundamental fear of the workhouse. It establishes her desire for independence and dignified death outside of parish charity—a central theme that drives her subsequent wanderings along the Thames valley and her desperate flight from officials seeking to place her under parish relief.
c41:p3: This chunk appears in the narrative about Old Betty Higden's journey after leaving Mr. Boffin's house. It describes her circumstances during her wanderings along the Thames—her determination to remain independent despite hardship, her unpaid debt for her traveling outfit, and her resolve to avoid the workhouse system that she fears and abhors. This passage establishes the conditions that drive her increasingly desperate pilgrimage as her health deteriorates.
c41:p4: This passage describes Betty Higden's declining health as she wanders the roads seeking work and charity. It explains that the "deadness" or fainting spells she previously mentioned to a secretary have grown increasingly frequent and severe, foreshadowing her physical deterioration during her journey along the Thames and subsequent encounters with parish officials.
c41:p5: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman fleeing the workhouse system, travels along the Thames River through various towns, selling her modest wares and knitting to survive while maintaining her independence and avoiding parish relief.
c41:p6: Betty Higden, an elderly pauper fleeing the workhouse system, travels along the Thames valley towns selling knitted goods and other trifles from her basket. This passage describes her daily routine and humble commerce in market-places and villages, where her neat appearance and cheerful manner lead locals to mistakenly believe she is wealthy, when in fact she struggles to survive while maintaining her independence and avoiding parish relief.
c41:p7: Betty Higden, an elderly pauper woman fleeing the workhouse system, travels along the Thames River through pleasant towns. This passage describes the natural beauty of the river landscape while depicting the river itself as a metaphorical voice offering her escape and death as an alternative to the cruel parish relief system she has spent her life trying to avoid.
c41:p8:
# Context: Betty Higden's Inner Thoughts During Her Wanderings

This passage captures Betty Higden's reflective observations and gentle musings as she travels through the pleasant Thames towns (Chertsey, Walton, Kingston, Staines), selling her wares. The narrator enters her untutored mind to reveal her compassionate ruminations on the genteel families in their fine houses, the humble laborers in their cottages, and shopkeepers at their trade. The passage emphasizes her lack of bitterness or envy despite her poverty, her memories of her dead child Johnny, and her stoic acceptance of hardship. These tender interior thoughts contrast sharply with her growing horror of the parish workhouse system that will be dramatized in the incidents that follow.
c41:p9: This passage describes Old Betty Higden's deepening despair and horror of the parish workhouse system as she travels along the Thames Valley. Weakened by illness, she witnesses the cruelty of poor relief officials and hears of deaths from poverty and exposure, which intensifies her determination to avoid falling into the hands of institutional "Charity" and to die free of parish control.
c41:p10: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman traveling along the Thames trying to survive independently, has developed an intense fear of parish workhouses and charitable relief. This passage explains her paradoxical terror of charity itself—she would rather flee in panic than accept help from authorities, viewing the welfare system as a threat to her dignity and freedom rather than aid.
c41:p11: Betty Higden's growing fear of the parish workhouse system intensifies after two frightening experiences during her travels along the Thames, as she flees from the charitable authorities she abhors.
c41:p12: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman fleeing the workhouse system, collapses in a market-place while selling her wares during her wandering pilgrimage along the Thames. The collapse is the first of two frightening incidents that intensify her terror of falling into the hands of parish charity.
c41:p13: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman traveling along the Thames, faints in a market-place. After recovering consciousness with the help of market-women, one asks if she is better and can manage on her own.
c41:p14: Old Betty Higden, a poor elderly woman traveling along the Thames to avoid the workhouse, faints in a marketplace. When she regains consciousness supported by kind market-women, she asks this question, not remembering her collapse.
c41:p15: Betty Higden collapses in a marketplace from the mysterious "deadness" afflicting her. When she regains consciousness, market women explain that she has experienced a fainting spell or fit, during which her body became stiff and numb rather than convulsive.
c41:p16: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman traveling alone along the Thames valley, faints in a marketplace. When she regains consciousness supported by kind market-women, she attributes her collapse to the recurring "numbness" or deadness that periodically overcomes her weakening body as she wanders seeking to avoid the workhouse.
c41:p17: Betty Higden has suffered a fainting spell in the marketplace and is being attended to by concerned market-women. When she recovers, they ask if the numbness that caused her collapse has passed.
c41:p18: Betty Higden recovers from a fainting spell in a market-place, reassuring the good-natured women who helped her that she is well enough to continue her journey, though she fears falling into the hands of parish charity.
c41:p19: Betty Higden collapses from weakness and illness in a market-place while selling her wares. Kind market-women help her recover from a fainting fit, though she remains unsteady on her feet. She insists she is well enough to continue her journey, but the women support her as she sits back down.
c41:p20: Betty Higden has collapsed in a marketplace from a fainting spell or fit. After being helped up by kind market-women, she reassures them that she is recovering and will be fine, though she remains weak and disoriented from the episode.
c41:p21: Old Betty Higden collapses from illness in a market-place. As concerned onlookers gather around her, farmers ask who her relatives are, fearing she needs care or assistance.
c41:p22: Betty Higden has collapsed from a fainting spell in a marketplace. Well-meaning bystanders gather around her, concerned about her welfare. A woman supporting her asks if she has family or acquaintances nearby, trying to determine if Betty has someone who can help her.
c41:p23: Betty Higden, an elderly vagrant woman, has collapsed in a marketplace and is being questioned by concerned onlookers about her family and whereabouts. When asked if she has people belonging to her, she assures them she does and urges them not to worry about her, desperate to hide her situation and avoid being reported to the parish authorities, whom she fears above all else.
c41:p24: Betty Higden has collapsed in a marketplace from a fainting spell. After being revived by kind-hearted market-women, concerned bystanders—both men and women—question her about whether she has family nearby, worried about her ability to travel alone in her weakened state.
c41:p25: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman traveling alone, has collapsed in a marketplace. Concerned bystanders are asking her where her family is and whether she's fit to travel. She reassures them that she has friends nearby and is well enough to continue on her way to London.
c41:p26: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman, has collapsed in a marketplace from exhaustion and illness. After kind bystanders help her up, they express concern about her condition and ability to travel, questioning her about her destination and attempting to persuade her to see a doctor—part of her growing fear of being forced into the workhouse system she has spent her life avoiding.
c41:p27: Betty Higden, an elderly pauper woman traveling the roads near the Thames, faints in a marketplace. When local people gather around her with concern, asking about her family and whether she's fit to travel, she insists she is well enough to continue to London where she has friends, desperately trying to reassure them so they won't involve the parish authorities—her greatest fear, as she has spent her life avoiding the workhouse.
c41:p28: Old Betty Higden, a poor elderly woman traveling alone and selling small wares, collapses in a marketplace. After being revived by kind women, she insists she is well enough to leave, but a bystander tries to prevent her departure, fearing she is unfit to travel and should see a parish doctor.
c41:p29: Betty Higden, a poor elderly woman traveling to avoid the workhouse, faints in a marketplace. When well-meaning bystanders try to help her and suggest she see a doctor or cannot travel, she panics, fearing they will report her to the parish authorities. She desperately flees from them, driven by her lifelong terror of being claimed by the Poor Law system.
c41:p30: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman traveling the roads to avoid the workhouse, faints in a marketplace. When she recovers, well-meaning townspeople and farmers become concerned about her welfare and suggest she needs medical attention. Desperate to escape their attempts to involve the parish authorities—whom she fears will force her into the workhouse—Betty flees in panic from the marketplace, running until she finds refuge in the woods.
c41:p31: Betty Higden, an elderly pauper fleeing the workhouse system, collapses by a riverbank while traveling. Weakened by illness and haunted by visions of her dead children, she loses consciousness and awakens in the Lock-house, where a Deputy Lock official questions her parish affiliation and threatens to turn her over to the parish authorities—intensifying her terror of the workhouse.
c41:p32: Old Betty Higden, a poor elderly woman fleeing the workhouse system, collapses by a river after a hallucinatory episode. She awakens in the Lock-house (a parish lock-up) where the Deputy Lock questions her about her origins and destination, beginning her interrogation about her parish settlement.
c41:p33: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman fleeing from workhouse authorities, collapses by a river after a confused vision. She awakens in the Lock-house (a parish office) and, disoriented and frightened, asks the Deputy Lock where she is.
c41:p34: Betty Higden, an elderly pauper fleeing the workhouse system, collapses by a river and loses consciousness. When she awakens, a man identifying himself as the Deputy Lock (an official of a canal lock-house) questions her about her parish and identity, threatening to report her to parish authorities unless she pays him her meager money to let her go.
c41:p35: Betty Higden has collapsed by a river and awakens in the Lock-house (a toll-keeper's residence). Confused and disoriented, she asks the Deputy Lock where she is, and he responds by identifying himself. Her fearful one-word question "The Lock?" reflects her growing alarm at being in the custody of a parish official, which threatens her desperate desire to avoid the workhouse.
c41:p36: Betty Higden, an elderly pauper fleeing the workhouse, has collapsed by a river lock and been brought inside by the Deputy Lock keeper. He now questions her about her parish of settlement, threatening to report her to parish authorities if she cannot pay for casual relief—a terrifying prospect for Betty, who has spent her life avoiding the workhouse system.
c41:p37: Old Betty Higden, a poor elderly woman fleeing the workhouse, faints by a river and is brought to a lock-keeper's house. Upon waking, the Deputy Lock questions her about her parish. At this moment, realizing she may be claimed by parish authorities who would strip her of her money and independence, she jumps from bed in panic, desperately searching for her basket to escape.
c41:p38: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman fleeing the workhouse system, collapses by a river and is brought to the Lock-house. The Deputy Lock questions her about her parish of settlement, explaining the harsh regulations of the Poor Law that will force her to be passed along as a "Casual" pauper to her home parish, threatening to seize her meager money.
c41:p39: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman traveling alone to avoid the workhouse, has collapsed near a river lock after experiencing a fainting spell. She awakens confused in the Lock-house, where the Deputy Lock questions her about her parish and circumstances, trying to determine if he should report her to the authorities. Betty attributes her collapse to the mysterious "deadness" that periodically overcomes her.
c41:p40: Betty Higden, an elderly pauper, has collapsed from exhaustion and illness while traveling to avoid the workhouse. The Deputy Lock at a lock-house has found her unconscious and brought her inside. He questions her about her condition and circumstances, warning her that parish authorities will demand payment and force her into the system she has spent her life avoiding.
c41:p41: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman fleeing from parish authority, tells the Deputy Lock that she has friends who can help her, hoping to convince him to let her leave the lock-house without being turned over to the parish.
c41:p42: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman fleeing the workhouse system, has collapsed and been brought to the Lock-house by the Deputy Lock. After questioning her about her parish and circumstances, he attempts to persuade her to surrender to parish authorities by warning her they will confiscate her money anyway. When she expresses her desperation to remain free of the parish system, he cynically advises her to contact her friends for help, then asks if she has any money—a prelude to extorting what little she has in exchange for letting her leave.
c41:p43: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman fleeing the workhouse system, has collapsed and been brought to the Lock-house by the Deputy Lock. When questioned about her resources, she admits to having only a small amount of money, which the Deputy Lock will later use to extort her into leaving without being reported to the parish authorities.
c41:p44: The Deputy Lock questions Betty Higden about her meager savings, warning her that parish authorities will confiscate her money if she continues on her way. This exchange occurs as Betty desperately tries to escape the workhouse system.
c41:p45: Old Betty Higden, a poor elderly woman fleeing from parish authority, is questioned by the Deputy Lock about her circumstances. When asked if she wants to keep her meager savings of money, she emphatically responds "Sure I do!" — expressing her determination to retain what little she has rather than have it taken by the parish officials.
c41:p46: Betty Higden, an elderly pauper fleeing the workhouse system, has collapsed and is discovered by the Deputy Lock at a lock-house by the river. She desperately wants to leave without being reported to the parish authorities, but the Deputy Lock warns her that if she continues, they will extract all her money from her as a Casual pauper before passing her to her Parish of settlement.
c41:p47: Betty Higden, an elderly pauper fleeing the workhouse system, has collapsed and been brought to the Lock-house by the Deputy Lock. When he warns her that parish authorities will take her money and force her into their system, she resolves to leave immediately rather than submit to the parish relief she has spent her life avoiding.
c41:p48: Betty Higden, an elderly vagrant woman fleeing poorhouse care, has collapsed and been brought to a lock-house by its deputy. The Deputy warns her that parish authorities will extract all her money for her relief and transfer to her home parish, intensifying her desperation to escape the parish system that she has spent her life avoiding.
c41:p49: Betty Higden, an elderly pauper fleeing the workhouse system, has collapsed and been found by the Deputy Lock at a lock-house by the river. After he warns her that parish authorities will take her money and force her into the system she has spent her life avoiding, she thanks him and attempts to leave, desperate to escape the parish relief she fears more than death.
c41:p50: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman fleeing the workhouse system, has collapsed at a lock-house and been brought inside by the Deputy Lock. As she attempts to leave to avoid being reported to parish authorities, the Deputy blocks her exit and questions her nervousness, beginning a manipulation that will ultimately result in him extorting her meager savings in exchange for allowing her to depart.
c41:p51: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman traveling along the Thames, has collapsed twice due to illness. After fainting in a marketplace and being questioned about her parish, she flees in terror. Later, she's found unconscious by a Deputy Lock (an official) at a lock-house. When he threatens to send her to the parish authorities, she desperately expresses her lifelong fear of the workhouse system and her determination to die as a free person, not under parish control.
c41:p52: Betty Higden, an elderly pauper fleeing the workhouse system, has collapsed near a lock-house and been brought inside by the Deputy Lock. Terrified of being turned over to parish authorities, she attempts to leave, but the Deputy Lock manipulates her with threats and moral arguments, using her fear of the parish system to extort money from her before reluctantly letting her go.
c41:p53: Betty Higden, an elderly pauper fleeing the workhouse system, has collapsed and been brought to a lock-house by the Deputy Lock. Desperate to avoid being turned over to parish authorities who will seize her meager savings and force her into the workhouse, she begs the Deputy Lock to let her go, offering him her money in exchange for her freedom.
c41:p54: Betty Higden, fleeing from parish authorities and the workhouse system, desperately appeals to the Deputy Lock by showing him a letter from her friends in London, hoping to convince him to let her leave without being handed over to the parish.
c41:p55: Old Betty Higden, a poor elderly woman fleeing from parish authority, has collapsed and been brought to a lock-house by the Deputy Lock. When questioned about her parish and threatened with forced relief, she desperately produces a letter from her friends to prove she has resources. The Deputy Lock examines the letter with an unreadable expression, revealing through his inability to read it that his apparent concern for protocol masks his true motive: extorting her meager money in exchange for her release.
c41:p56: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman fleeing the workhouse system, has collapsed and been brought to the Lock-house by its Deputy. She desperately wants to leave to avoid being handed over to the Parish authorities. The Deputy Lock, exploiting her fear and desperation, questions her about her money to extract a bribe in exchange for letting her go.
c41:p57: Betty Higden, fleeing from the workhouse system her entire life, is caught by the Deputy Lock after collapsing. Desperate to escape being handed over to the parish authorities, she offers him all her money—a shilling, two sixpenny pieces, and a few pence—as a bribe to let her go free.
c41:p58: Betty Higden, an elderly poor woman fleeing the workhouse system, has collapsed and been brought to the Lock-house by the Deputy Lock. Desperate to avoid being processed by the parish authorities who would seize her money and belongings, she attempts to leave. The Deputy Lock now attempts to extort her small savings by implying he could report her to the parish, using this quoted statement to manipulate her into voluntarily surrendering her money in exchange for her freedom.
c41:p59: Betty Higden, an elderly pauper fleeing from the parish system, is intercepted by the Deputy Lock at a lock-house. After he threatens to turn her over to the parish authorities unless she pays him, she desperately offers him all her meager savings—a shilling, two sixpenny pieces, and a few pence—to let her go free.
c41:p60: Betty Higden, an elderly pauper fleeing the parish system, collapses on the road and is brought to the Lock-house by the Deputy Lock. After discovering her condition and learning she has money, the Deputy Lock threatens to turn her over to the parish authorities unless she pays him. Betty, desperate to avoid the workhouse and die free of parish control, tearfully surrenders her meager savings. The Deputy, having extracted a bribe, releases her with this final condescending remark about earning his living honestly.
c42:p0: This is the opening passage of the chapter, depicting the funeral service of Betty Higden, an elderly pauper who has died. The Reverend Frank Milvey reads the burial service while reflecting on the irony and tragedy of how society treats its poor through the Poor Law system. The passage establishes the somber tone and introduces themes of death, poverty, and social injustice that frame the subsequent events of the chapter.
c42:p1: This passage occurs at the funeral of Betty Higden, an elderly woman who served as a maternal figure to Sloppy, a poor orphan she had cared for. Sloppy struggles to feel grateful for her death (which the funeral service celebrates as deliverance from suffering) because he is overwhelmed with grief and guilt, unable to muster the expected thankfulness despite understanding intellectually that her death freed her from hardship. The narrator sympathizes with this emotional contradiction, noting that Sloppy's selfish grief is forgivable given Betty's profound maternal role in his life.
c42:p2: This passage occurs during Betty Higden's burial service at an obscure, unmarked churchyard near the river. The Reverend Frank Milvey has just read the funeral rites over her ashes. The narrator then digresses into social commentary about the lack of proper grave markers for the poor and working classes, advocating for a system to identify graves so that families might locate their deceased relatives. This meditation reflects on society's indifference to memorializing the common people despite claims of equality in death.
c42:p3: This passage describes the mourners gathered at Betty Higden's funeral in a remote churchyard. It establishes that despite her poverty, Betty's wish to be buried without becoming a burden on the Poor Law has been honored—the money she had sewn into her dress for her burial expenses remains untouched, signifying that her independent spirit and final wishes have been respected.
c42:p4: Sloppy grieves at Betty Higden's funeral, expressing regret that he may not have worked hard enough for her during her life, as the burial service concludes at an obscure churchyard by the river.
c42:p5: At Betty Higden's funeral service, the Reverend Frank Milvey consoles a grieving Sloppy by offering philosophical comfort about human moral failings, using the metaphor of turning mangles to suggest that all people are imperfect in fulfilling their duties.
c42:p6: At Betty Higden's funeral, the Reverend Frank Milvey attempts to comfort the grieving Sloppy by explaining that all people fall short in their duties. Sloppy vehemently rejects this consolation, insisting that Mrs. Higden was different—she faithfully fulfilled every obligation and responsibility, and he celebrates her memory as an exceptional woman, mother, and laundress.
c42:p7: This passage occurs at the funeral of Betty Higden, following Sloppy's emotional eulogy praising her industriousness and devotion. The Reverend Frank Milvey comments on the dignity and richness of her humble grave, elevated by Sloppy's genuine grief and tribute to her character.
c42:p8: This passage occurs after Betty Higden's funeral service at an obscure churchyard. The mourners—Reverend Frank Milvey, his wife, John Rokesmith (the Secretary), Bella Wilfer, and Sloppy—have just left the graveside where Sloppy wept for his beloved benefactress. As they depart the churchyard, Lizzie Hexam recounts to them the circumstances of Betty Higden's death: how she heard her groans, what transpired afterward, and how she secured permission to temporarily house the body in the paper-mill's storage room before its burial. The passage marks the transition from the funeral rites to the group's interaction with Lizzie, who will become central to the remainder of the chapter.
c42:p9: Lizzie Hexam explains to the mourners at Betty Higden's funeral that she could not have arranged the burial and funeral rites without the help of her employer, the managing partner of the paper-mill. This follows her account of how she obtained permission to place Betty's remains in the mill's store-room before the funeral service.
c42:p10: Mrs. Milvey expresses surprise and concern upon learning that Lizzie Hexam's "managing partner" at the paper-mill—the person who has greatly helped her with Betty Higden's burial arrangements—is Jewish. The remark reveals Mrs. Milvey's prejudice and her immediate worry about Jewish influence on Lizzie's Christian faith.
c42:p11: Mrs. Milvey expresses surprise that Lizzie Hexam's managing partner at the paper mill is Jewish, and her husband gently questions her prejudiced reaction, suggesting there is nothing inherently wrong with a Jewish employer.
c42:p12: This exchange occurs during Mrs. Milvey's conversation with Lizzie Hexam about her employers at the paper mill. Mrs. Milvey expresses concern that Lizzie's Jewish employers might try to convert her to their religion, but Lizzie defends them as kind and respectful people who do not interfere with anyone's faith and simply treat their employees well.
c42:p13: Mrs. Milvey expresses concern that the Jewish couple employing Lizzie Hexam might attempt to convert her to their religion, revealing prejudiced assumptions about Jewish people despite Lizzie's positive experiences working for them.
c42:p14: Mrs. Milvey expresses concern that Lizzie's Jewish employers might try to convert her from Christianity. Lizzie responds with confusion, asking what conversion would mean.
c42:p15: Mrs Milvey expresses concern that the Jewish couple employing Lizzie Hexam might attempt to convert her to their religion, though Lizzie reassures her that they respect everyone's faith and have never tried to interfere with hers.
c42:p16: This passage is Lizzie Hexam's response to Mrs. Milvey's concerns about the Jewish owners of the paper mill where Lizzie works. Lizzie defends her employers' character and their respectful treatment of their workers, emphasizing that they focus on practical matters like diligence and faithfulness rather than attempting religious conversion. The exchange occurs during the group's visit to the mill village following Betty Higden's funeral.
c42:p17: Mrs. Milvey expresses mild displeasure upon learning that Lizzie Hexam has earned a position of confidence at the paper-mill through the kindness of her Jewish employers, who treat her with particular favor and consideration.
c42:p18: Lizzie Hexam defends her Jewish employers to Mrs. Milvey, who expresses concern that they might try to convert her. Lizzie praises their respectful treatment and explains that they never impose their religion on their employees, nor do they inquire about the religion of others, including the recently deceased Betty Higden.
c42:p19: Mrs. Milvey expresses concern to her husband about Lizzie Hexam's close relationship with her Jewish employers and fears they may try to convert her to their faith, prompting her to urge the Reverend Frank to intervene and counsel Lizzie on the matter.
c42:p20: The Reverend Frank Milvey declines his wife's request to persuade Lizzie Hexam to convert to Christianity, reasoning that circumstances are unsuitable and that she will encounter other religious advocates without his intervention.
c42:p21: This passage occurs during the conversation between the Reverend and Mrs. Milvey, Bella, and the Secretary at Lizzie Hexam's lodgings following Betty Higden's funeral. It marks the moment when John Harmon (disguised as the Secretary) and Bella both observe Lizzie for the first time, each with hidden reasons for their interest—Harmon because her father was falsely accused of murdering him, and Bella because she was intended to marry the supposed victim. The passage explains how their mutual attention to Lizzie creates an unspoken connection between them.
c42:p22: This chunk occurs at the moment when the group visiting Lizzie Hexam's lodging by the paper-mill departs, leaving Bella and the Secretary alone together in the village street. The mill bell's ringing creates an opportunity for private conversation between them, away from the Milveys' scrutiny. This encounter becomes significant as it allows Bella and the Secretary to discuss their shared concerns about Lizzie's circumstances and Mr. Boffin's changing behavior, marking a turning point in their relationship and understanding of each other.
c42:p23: After visiting Lizzie Hexam's cottage and observing her along with the Secretary, Bella and the Secretary find themselves alone together on a wooded path by the river. Standing awkwardly in the small village street while the Reverend and Mrs. Milvey are occupied elsewhere, Bella breaks the silence to initiate a conversation about their shared commission to report on Lizzie Hexam to the Boffins.
c42:p24: After visiting Lizzie Hexam's lodging and observing her with great attention, Bella and the Secretary find themselves alone on the wooded landscape by the river. Initially constrained and formal with each other, they begin to speak more naturally. Bella then brings up the purpose of their visit—the commission Mr. Boffin has given them to investigate whether the false accusation against Lizzie's father has any bearing on her request to keep her whereabouts secret.
c42:p25: Bella asks the Secretary to discuss their commission regarding Lizzie Hexam, and he readily agrees to do so.
c42:p26: Bella questions whether she and the Secretary have both been given the same commission by Mr. and Mrs. Boffin to investigate Lizzie Hexam and report on her circumstances, particularly regarding the false accusation against her father.
c42:p27: Bella asks the Secretary if they are both commissioned by Mr. and Mrs. Boffin to report on Lizzie Hexam, and he briefly confirms this supposition with "I suppose so."
c42:p28: Bella explains to the Secretary her reason for accompanying the Milveys to visit Lizzie Hexam, revealing that Mrs Boffin commissioned her to observe and report on Lizzie, while the Secretary has been similarly commissioned by Mr Boffin.
c42:p29: After Betty Higden's funeral, the Secretary and Bella Wilfer are commissioned by Mr. and Mrs. Boffin to observe and report on Lizzie Hexam. The Secretary confirms he has been given the same task by Mr. Boffin as Bella has been given by Mrs. Boffin.
c42:p30: John Rokesmith and Bella Wilfer have just finished discussing their commission to investigate Lizzie Hexam's circumstances, and as they walk together away from the village, they transition from their stilted conversation to more natural, warm interaction.
c42:p31: After Betty Higden's funeral, Bella and the Secretary (John Rokesmith) walk together by the river near the paper-mill where Lizzie Hexam works. As they discuss their shared commission to report on Lizzie to Mr. Boffin, Bella initiates conversation about Lizzie's appearance and character, seeking the Secretary's opinion while being conscious of making the romantic overtures in their exchange.
c42:p32: Rokesmith expresses his favorable opinion of Lizzie Hexam to Bella Wilfer as they walk by the river after Betty Higden's funeral, during their conversation about the task Mr. Boffin has assigned them to investigate Lizzie's circumstances.
c42:p33: Bella remarks on Lizzie Hexam's refined beauty while walking with the Secretary by the river, after they have visited Betty Higden's grave and agreed to investigate Lizzie's reasons for secrecy.
c42:p34: Bella and the Secretary (John Rokesmith) discuss Lizzie Hexam after visiting her at the paper-mill cottage. The Secretary makes this brief, reserved comment about Lizzie's appearance while they walk together by the river, as Bella attempts to draw him out into more natural conversation.
c42:p35: Bella and the Secretary are walking by the river after Betty Higden's funeral and discussing their impressions of Lizzie Hexam. Bella comments on the sadness she observes in Lizzie's appearance, seeking the Secretary's validation of her observation.

In this tender, intimate moment between father and daughter, Bella playfully shares a fortune that was told to her on her way home, using the third-person phrase "the lovely woman" to refer to herself. She describes her future marriage on modest means and hints at a special place in her heart for a certain fair, little man—clearly referring to her father—suggesting he will always have a cherished corner in her future home.
c49:p166: Bella tells her father about a fortune-teller's prediction that a "fair man—a little man" will always have a peaceful corner in her future home. Her father playfully responds by asking if this man is a Knave in a deck of cards, with a knowing twinkle in his eye, teasing her about the mysterious figure in her fortune.
c50:p0: This is the opening passage of the chapter, introducing the financial ruin of Mr. and Mrs. Alfred Lammle and the Veneerings' hypocritical response to it. The Veneerings, despite their dubious reputation, immediately claim the Lammles as their oldest and dearest friends and decide to host a "wondering dinner" to discuss the scandal among their social circle.
c50:p1: This passage describes the Veneerings' obsessive habit of hosting elaborate dinners as a response to any social circumstance. It establishes their compulsive entertaining practices and the true nature of their dinner guests' motivations—they attend to socialize with each other rather than to honor their hosts. This occurs early in the chapter as context for the "wondering dinner" being held to respond to the Lammles' financial ruin.
c50:p2: This passage appears in paragraph P2 and discusses Mr. Podsnap's vanity and concern for his social reputation. It explains how Veneering's expensive dinners function as a form of social capital, using the metaphor of ornamental camels on the Veneering table to illustrate how guests like Podsnap protect their own dignity by supporting the dignity of those they associate with. The passage satirizes upper-class concern with appearances and the fear that association with questionable people might reflect poorly on oneself.
c50:p3: The Veneerings are preparing a dinner to address the mysterious financial collapse of the Lammles. Mr. Twemlow, a meek and socially anxious gentleman, is at his modest lodgings feeling unwell from digestive pills when Mrs. Lammle unexpectedly arrives to speak with him about a sensitive confidential matter from their past.
c50:p4: Mrs. Lammle, facing financial ruin, arrives unannounced at Twemlow's lodgings to remind him of a confidence she previously shared with him and to warn him against using that knowledge against her or her husband. When the servant announces a lady wishes to see him, Twemlow, recovering from the effects of advertised pills, asks for the visitor's name before agreeing to receive her.
c50:p5: Mrs. Lammle arrives unannounced at Mr. Twemlow's lodgings to speak with him privately about a sensitive matter related to their previous conversation and her husband's financial ruin. She seeks to remind him of confidential information she had entrusted to him and to establish that he must maintain strict neutrality regarding her affairs.
c50:p6: Mr. Twemlow receives an unexpected visitor at his lodgings in Duke Street, Saint James's. After a servant announces that a lady wishes to speak with him, Twemlow requests her name. The servant delivers multiple assurances that the lady (Mrs. Lammle) is certain Mr. Twemlow will see her, and she has no card to send in. Twemlow then agrees to receive her, leading to this brief stage direction indicating her entrance.
c50:p7: This passage describes Mr. Twemlow's modest lodgings in Duke Street, Saint James's, where Mrs. Lammle has come to visit him unexpectedly. The detailed description of his sparsely furnished rooms and the prominent engraving of Lord Snigsworth establishes the setting before their important conversation about the Lammles' financial ruin and Mrs. Lammle's warning regarding Mr. Fledgeby.

# Context for Chunk

Mr. Twemlow invites Mrs. Lammle to sit down in his modest rooms at his lodgings in Duke Street, Saint James's, after she has unexpectedly called upon him. She has come to remind him of a confidence she previously shared with him regarding her husband's affairs, and to request his strict neutrality regarding the knowledge she entrusted to him. This marks the beginning of their private conversation about the Lammles' financial ruin and her concerns about Mr. Fledgeby.
c50:p9: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to discuss the Lammles' financial ruin and bankruptcy, which has become public knowledge through the auction of their furniture.
c50:p10: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to discuss the financial ruin that has befallen the Lammles. Twemlow acknowledges having heard of their reversed fortune, reluctantly admitting it in light of the Veneerings' planned dinner to address the Lammles' downfall.
c50:p11: Mrs Lammle visits Mr Twemlow at his lodgings to follow up on a previous private conversation about the Lammles' financial ruin. She warns him not to use information she previously shared with him in confidence against her or her husband, and seeks his neutrality regarding their affairs.
c50:p12: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she previously shared with him regarding Mr. Fledgeby and his deceptive character. c50:p13: Twemlow, visited unexpectedly by Mrs. Lammle at his lodgings, becomes anxious when she hints at discussing a previous confidence between them. c50:p14: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she previously shared with him regarding the Lammles' financial ruin. c50:p15: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a previous confidence she had shared with him regarding the Lammles' financial troubles. c50:p17: Mrs Lammle visits Mr Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she had previously shared with him about the Lammles' financial ruin. c50:p18: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a secret she previously entrusted to him about the Lammles' financial ruin. c50:p19: Mrs Lammle visits Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she had previously shared with him about her husband, which he had passed on to another person as she had requested.
c50:p20: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she previously shared with him regarding a specific matter involving a girl. c50:p21: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him that he must not use against her and her husband the confidential information she previously shared with him about their deception. c50:p22: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidential matter she previously shared with him. c50:p23: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she had previously shared with him about the Lammles' financial ruin. c50:p24: Mr Twemlow, recovering his composure after Mrs Lammle's visit regarding the Lammles' financial ruin, challenges her about an apparent inconsistency: she had previously resolved with him to take action against the moneylender Mr Fledgeby, yet afterwards approached Fledgeby as a friend asking for his help. c50:p25: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she previously shared with him regarding Mr. Fledgeby. c50:p26: This single-word affirmation occurs in paragraph P26, where Twemlow confirms to Mrs. Lammle that Mr. Fledgeby told him the truth about her approaching Fledgeby as a confidential friend after they had made a resolution against him. c50:p27: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she had previously shared with him regarding Mr. Fledgeby. c50:p28: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she previously shared with him regarding Mr. Fledgeby. c50:p29: Mrs Lammle is questioning Mr Twemlow about where he encountered Mr Fledgeby, seeking to confirm her suspicion that Fledgeby is actually the money lender Mr Riah operating behind a mask. She asks this after Twemlow has hesitated to reveal the location of his meeting with Fledgeby.
c50:p30: Twemlow reveals to Mrs. Lammle that he encountered Fledgeby at Riah's in Saint Mary Axe, where Twemlow himself is indebted. Twemlow confesses his discomfort about how Fledgeby treated him civilly while assisting him with the same financial favor Fledgeby had provided to Mrs. Lammle.
c50:p31: Mr. Twemlow is speaking with Mrs. Lammle about her financial troubles and Mr. Fledgeby's involvement in lending matters. When admitting his own debt to Riah (actually Fledgeby), Twemlow reveals that Fledgeby had done him the same service he had done for Mrs. Lammle. This internal reflection shows Twemlow's moral consideration: he mentions his own difficulties not to diminish hers, but to acknowledge shared hardship with integrity rather than claiming superiority.
c50:p32: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she previously shared with him about Mr. Fledgeby being involved in questionable financial dealings. During their conversation, Twemlow reveals that he too has sought Fledgeby's help with a money matter, and Mrs. Lammle questions whether Fledgeby's assistance was as unsuccessful for him as it was for the Lammles.
c50:p33: Mrs Lammle questions Mr Twemlow about whether Mr Fledgeby's advocacy was as effective in helping resolve Twemlow's financial difficulties as it was in resolving her own, to which Twemlow replies that Fledgeby's efforts were equally ineffective in both cases.
c50:p34: Mrs Lammle visits Mr Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she previously shared with him regarding Mr Fledgeby. During their conversation, she discovers that Twemlow has also encountered Fledgeby and seeks the location of their meeting.
c50:p35: Mr. Twemlow reveals to Mrs. Lammle that he encountered Mr. Fledgeby by accident at Mr. Riah's office in Saint Mary Axe, where Twemlow's own debt has fallen into Riah's hands. This disclosure occurs during Mrs. Lammle's visit to Twemlow's lodgings, where she warns him about the true nature of Mr. Riah's relationship to Fledgeby and cautions him against being deceived by appearances.
c50:p36: Mrs Lammle visits Mr Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she previously shared with him regarding Mr Fledgeby. Twemlow then admits that he himself is indebted to Mr Riah, prompting Mrs Lammle's inquiry about whether he is unfortunate enough to be in Mr Riah's hands.
c50:p37: Mrs Lammle visits Mr Twemlow to remind him of their previous confidence regarding Mr Fledgeby and to warn him against using that knowledge against her and her husband. During this conversation, Twemlow reveals that he is indebted to Mr Riah, a moneylender.
c50:p38: Mrs Lammle visits Mr Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a previous confidence she shared and to warn him about Mr Fledgeby. She reveals that Mr Riah is merely Fledgeby's front, and Twemlow's debt has actually fallen into Fledgeby's hands, not Riah's. She urges him to use this information to avoid being deceived by Fledgeby's false claims of truthfulness.
c50:p39: Mrs. Lammle reveals to Twemlow that Mr. Riah is actually a mask for Mr. Fledgeby, who truly holds Twemlow's debt. Twemlow expresses shock and disbelief at this revelation, asking how she could possibly know such information.
c50:p40: Mrs Lammle explains to Mr Twemlow how she discovered that Mr Riah is merely a mask for Mr Fledgeby, the true money-lender behind Twemlow's debt. She asserts she has no formal proof, only intuition based on circumstantial evidence.
c50:p41: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow to remind him not to use against her and her husband the confidential information she previously shared with him. When she claims that Mr. Riah is actually Mr. Fledgeby's mask, Twemlow challenges her assertion by asking for proof, to which she responds dismissively that she has none, only circumstantial evidence.
c50:p42: Mrs Lammle visits Mr Twemlow to remind him of a confidence she shared with him earlier and to warn him that Mr Riah is actually a mask for Mr Fledgeby. When Twemlow questions her claim by saying she has no proof, Mrs Lammle expresses frustration that both her husband and Twemlow respond identically, noting the irony that two such different men share the same skeptical response.
c50:p43: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow to remind him not to use against her and her husband the confidential information she previously shared with him. When she claims that Mr. Riah is actually Mr. Fledgeby's mask, Twemlow skeptically objects that she has no proof, to which she responds by noting that both he and her husband make the same objection—a sign of masculine weakness in reasoning.
c50:p44: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him not to use against her and her husband the confidential information she previously shared with him. During their conversation, Twemlow confronts her about approaching Fledgeby after they had agreed to take action against him. Mrs. Lammle responds by revealing her conviction that Fledgeby is actually the mask behind Mr. Riah, the moneylender, and insists that despite lacking proof, women would perceive this truth more readily than men. She vows to make her husband see it as well, even though she cannot provide evidence.
c50:p45: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she previously shared with him about Mr. Fledgeby, warning him not to use this knowledge against her or her husband. She also reveals to Twemlow that Mr. Fledgeby is actually the masked owner behind Mr. Riah, the moneylender. As Mrs. Lammle prepares to leave after their tense conversation, Mr. Twemlow attempts to comfort her by expressing hope that her husband's financial situation might still be recoverable.
c50:p46: Mrs Lammle visits Mr Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she previously shared and to extract a promise of his neutrality regarding her and her husband's affairs. After discussing Mr Fledgeby and Mr Riah, and expressing her conviction that Fledgeby is behind Riah's moneylending operations, the conversation turns to the Lammles' financial ruin. As Mrs Lammle prepares to leave, Mr Twemlow expresses hope that Mr Lammle's affairs might be retrievable, prompting her response about their possible bankruptcy and potential need to go abroad.
c50:p47: Mrs Lammle has just told Mr Twemlow that if her husband's financial affairs cannot be salvaged, they may have to go bankrupt and relocate abroad. Twemlow attempts to console her by optimistically suggesting that people can live pleasantly in foreign countries.
c50:p48: Mrs Lammle visits Mr Twemlow to remind him not to use confidential information she previously shared about her husband's financial dealings. After discussing their financial ruin, Twemlow remarks that pleasant lives can be found abroad, to which Mrs Lammle responds skeptically about the quality of such lives, doubting whether living by gambling and card-playing at disreputable establishments constitutes a pleasant existence.
c50:p49: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of a confidence she had shared with him and to ensure his neutrality regarding her husband's affairs. After revealing that Mr. Riah is actually Mr. Fledgeby's mask, she discusses the Lammles' financial ruin and their uncertain prospects. Twemlow attempts to console her by suggesting that having a devoted spouse to restrain her husband from ruinous conduct is admirable, prompting Mrs. Lammle's bitter response about the reality of their marriage built on mutual deception.
c50:p50: Mrs. Lammle, visiting Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to warn him about Mr. Fledgeby's deception, responds bitterly to Twemlow's sympathetic comment about her husband having a restraining influence. She expresses her cynical view of her marriage, revealing that she and her husband married under mutual deception and are now trapped together by financial necessity and circumstance, condemned to scheme for their daily survival until death.
c50:p51: Mrs. Lammle visits Mr. Twemlow at his lodgings to remind him of their previous confidential agreement and warn him that Mr. Riah is actually a mask for Mr. Fledgeby. After an intense confrontation where Mrs. Lammle reveals her bitter circumstances—her marriage based on mutual deception and her precarious financial situation—she departs, leaving the weakened and troubled Twemlow to recover on his sofa before attending the Veneerings' wondering dinner that evening.
c50:p52: Mr. Twemlow recovers from his distressing interview with Mrs. Lammle, during which she warned him not to use against the Lammles the confidential information she had previously shared with him. After she departs, he rests on his sofa, feeling unwell from the dinner pills he had taken. By evening, he recovers sufficiently to prepare himself for the Veneerings' dinner party, where guests have gathered to discuss and speculate about the Lammles' financial ruin.
c50:p53: This passage occurs at the Veneerings' dinner party held to discuss the financial ruin of the Lammles. c50:p54: This passage appears in the context of the "wondering dinner" at the Veneerings' house, held to address the scandal of the Lammles' financial ruin. The chunk describes the nouveau riche guests whom Veneering has cultivated since entering Parliament—wealthy financiers and businessmen referred to as the "Fathers of the Scrip-Church." It satirizes their inflated social importance through exaggerated claims about their business operations and wealth, while showing how Veneering courts their favor through conspiratorial discussions in the conservatory. This occurs midway through the dinner scene, before the main conversation turns to discussing the Lammles' downfall.
c50:p55: This passage occurs at the Veneering dinner party held to discuss the Lammles' financial ruin. The Veneerings have invited wealthy and important guests, including Mr. Podsnap and his wife, as well as Lady Tippins and various wealthy "Fathers" (influential businessmen). The chunk marks the transition point where, after some social pleasantries and discussion about navvies, the company refocuses on the main purpose of the dinner: to wonder about and discuss how the Lammles came to financial ruin. Brewer is about to initiate this discussion by revealing he attended the auction of their furniture.

c50:p57: During the Veneerings' dinner party to discuss the Lammles' financial ruin, Brewer mentions attending an auction of the Lammles' furniture that morning. Boots enviously claims he also attended the same sale.

c50:p59: At the Veneerings' dinner gathering, Brewer recounts visiting an auction sale of the Lammles' furniture after their financial ruin. Veneering asks Brewer to describe what he witnessed at the sale.

c50:p64: At the wondering dinner held by the Veneerings to discuss the Lammles' financial ruin, Veneering expresses bewilderment at how anyone could live beyond their means, prompting general agreement from the dinner guests about the incomprehensibility of the Lammles' financial collapse.
c50:p65: The Veneerings host a dinner to discuss the Lammles' financial ruin. c50:p66: At the Veneerings' wondering dinner, guests speculate about how the Lammles could have suffered financial ruin. Mrs. Veneering poses a rhetorical question about how a mother could knowingly allow her family to live beyond their means, suggesting moral culpability in the Lammles' downfall.
c50:p67: At the Veneerings' dinner party, guests speculate about how the Lammles came to financial ruin. c50:p68: Mrs. Veneering defends her argument that Mrs. Lammle, as a woman, should have known better than to live beyond her husband's means, even without a baby to look at. c50:p70: A wealthy businessman questions how the Lammles, who were clearly members of society and had dined at the Veneerings' home, could have suffered such a complete financial collapse.
c50:p71: The Veneerings are hosting a dinner to discuss the financial ruin of the Lammles. c50:p72: At the Veneerings' wondering dinner, one of the wealthy "Fathers of the Scrip-Church" questions how the Lammles' financial ruin could be so complete, arguing that people of social standing typically have means to adjust their affairs rather than face total bankruptcy.
c50:p73: At the Veneerings' dinner party, guests speculate about how the Lammles came to financial ruin. c50:p74: This chunk occurs during the "wondering dinner" at the Veneerings' house, where guests speculate about the causes of the Lammles' financial ruin. c50:p75: Mr. Podsnap, a representative man of society, refuses to discuss the Lammles' financial ruin at the Veneerings' wondering dinner. c50:p76: This chunk occurs during the Veneerings' "wondering dinner," after Mr. Podsnap has angrily dismissed discussion of the Lammles' financial ruin.
